result.summary: Phaëton goes to the palace of Apollo, here called Phœbus and the Sun, and asks for proof that he is his son. Apollo swears by the Styx to grant any gift, and Phaëton demands to drive the sun's chariot for a day. Apollo warns him in vain, and when the horses bolt the world catches fire until Earth begs Jupiter to save it.

scenes.title: The Palace of the Sun
scenes.summary: The splendid palace of the Sun is described, with its carvings of sea, earth and heaven. Phaëton enters and stands before his father's throne, attended by the Days, Months, Years and Seasons.

scenes.title: The Oath by the Styx
scenes.summary: Phœbus asks why Phaëton has come. Phaëton asks for a token of his parentage, and Phœbus embraces him and swears to grant any gift.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton's standing as Phœbus's son and his claim to be believed.

scenes.title: Apollo's Warning
scenes.summary: Phaëton asks for the chariot. Phœbus regrets his oath and lists the dangers of the road, but Phaëton persists and is led to the chariot.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton risks his life by insisting on a task beyond mortal strength.

scenes.title: Dawn and Departure
scenes.summary: Dawn breaks as Phaëton admires the chariot. Phœbus anoints his face, advises him on the course, and Phaëton mounts.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton's life, if he strays from the oblique track or loses control.

scenes.title: The Horses Run Wild
scenes.summary: The light chariot lurches, and the horses leave their track. Phaëton panics at the sight of the Scorpion and drops the reins.
scenes.stakes: Phaëton faces death in the sky and the horses' bolting threatens the whole world.

scenes.title: The World Burns
scenes.summary: The runaway chariot sets mountains, cities, rivers and seas ablaze. Peoples change colour, rivers dry up, and the sea shrinks.
scenes.stakes: All the earth, its peoples and waters face destruction by fire.

scenes.title: Earth's Plea to Jupiter
scenes.summary: Earth, scorched and barely able to speak, pleads with Jupiter to save the universe, or at least to destroy her with his own bolts.
scenes.stakes: The universe would fall back into chaos if Earth, sea and heaven perish.

alias_notes.explanation: The text uses Apollo, Phœbus, the Sun and Titan for the sun god.
Epithet for Jupiter as king of the gods.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo's blunt warning that Phaëton's request exceeds mortal limits.
Apollo says his fearful concern is the proof of fatherhood.
Earth warns that the universe will fall back into ancient chaos.

analysis.text: The passage shows the danger of youthful ambition and of rash vows. Apollo cannot take back his oath by the Styx, so a foolish wish brings catastrophe.
The catalogue of burning mountains and rivers displays Ovid's learned geography and reflects Roman interest in a world united under one empire, including the Tiber promised world rule.

legacy.text: The Phaëton myth became a standard image of reckless ambition. It gave the word phaeton to a light open carriage, and inspired artists and poets such as Rubens and Milton's age.

fun_facts.text: The ancients offered the myth as an explanation for the dark skin of Ethiopians and for the Libyan desert.

language_notes.text: Carbuncle is a red gemstone, such as garnet, polished into a rounded shape; it was thought to glow like a coal.
Mulciber is a name for Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), the smith-god who made the palace's carvings.
Proteus was a sea-god who could change shape at will, which explains the epithet 'changing'.
'Thus doubted of' means that Phaëton's parentage was in question, since Epaphus had mocked his claim to be the Sun's son.
Refulgence means radiant brightness.
'Corn' here means grain, especially wheat, not maize.
"Use of that name" means the right to call Phœbus father; Phaëton doubts his parentage because Clymene, his mother, claims it.
The lake is the river Styx in the underworld; an oath by the Styx was the gods' most binding and could not be broken.
"By thine" means by your words: Phaëton's own request has made Phœbus's promise a rash one.
"Axle-tree" is the axle of the chariot, which carries the sun across the sky.
Tethys is a sea goddess, wife of Oceanus; the sun was imagined setting into her waters.
The Bull, Hæmonian bow (Sagittarius, the centaur archer), Lion, Scorpion and Crab are zodiac constellations that the sun's path crosses.
"Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning "indeed", here used sarcastically.
Chrysolites are golden-yellow gemstones, probably what we now call topaz or peridot.
Lucifer is the morning star (Venus), 'light-bringer', who leads the stars away last at dawn; not the Christian Satan.
Titan here means the Sun god Phœbus, descended from the Titans; the Hours are goddesses of the divisions of time.
Ambrosia is the food of the gods, here nourishing the horses of the Sun.
The five circles are the celestial zones; the footnote refers to them. Phœbus tells Phaëton to avoid the direct paths and keep to the oblique zodiac track.
The Serpent (Draco) and the Altar (Ara) are constellations marking the northern and southern limits of the safe path.
'Touched the goals' means Night has reached the western end of her course; the sun must now begin his.
Pyroeis, Eoüs, Æthon and Phlegon are the names of the sun's horses, meaning roughly fiery, dawn-like, blazing and burning.
Tethys, a sea goddess and wife of Oceanus, is Phaëton's grandmother, since the Sun's father figure belongs to her family. She opens the barriers unaware of the danger.
The Triones are the seven stars of the Great and Little Bear. They never set in the sea, so being 'forbidden' to dip refers to that myth.
Boötes, the 'Ox-driver' constellation, follows the Wain (the Plough or Wagon). The slow wagon was proverbial for sluggish motion.
Merops was the mortal husband of Clymene, Phaëton's mother. Phaëton now wishes he had stayed known as Merops' son, not the Sun's.
The Scorpion constellation (Scorpio) was so large that its claws were once drawn to occupy two zodiac signs, later Libra.
The narrator breaks off the catalogue of damage, saying these are small losses beside what follows, to prepare for larger destruction.
Hæmus is 'not yet called Œagrian' because it was later linked with Orpheus, son of Œagrus; the poet looks ahead to that later name.
Ovid gives a mythic explanation for the dark skin of Ethiopians, an ancient 'origin story' not a factual account.
Dirce, Amymone and Pirene are famous springs near Thebes (Bœotia), Argos and Corinth (Ephyre); each place mourns its own water.
The Tiber is promised world sovereignty because its city, Rome, would one day rule the known world.
Tartarus is the deep part of the underworld; the Infernal King and his spouse are Pluto and Proserpina, rulers of the dead.
Nereus and Doris are sea deities; their daughters are the Nereids, sea nymphs.
"Genial" here means generative or life-giving; "all-productive" is likewise an epithet for Earth as bearer of all growth. "Main" means the open sea.
Earth asks that if she must die by fire, it be by Jupiter's own thunderbolts, so that he at least takes responsibility for her destruction.
Jupiter's brother is Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), ruler of the sea, which was allotted to him when the brothers divided the world.
Atlas was the Titan condemned to hold up the sky on his shoulders.
Ancient chaos is the formless, undivided mass that existed before the world was ordered, described in Book 1.

context_notes.text: Triton was a sea-god who blew a conch shell to calm or raise the waves. Doris was a sea-goddess, mother of the Nereids.
The twelve Zodiac signs are split six per door, which suggests the sky's yearly circuit.
Phœbus is a title of Apollo as the Sun; this translation uses Apollo and Phœbus for the same god.
Phœbus is the sun god, also called Apollo. The sun sees everything, as the phrase "eyes with which he beholds all things" recalls.
Jupiter is king of the gods and wields the thunderbolt. Phœbus argues that even he cannot drive the sun's chariot.
Vulcan is the smith god who forged the sun's chariot.
Aurora is the goddess of dawn, whose palace in the east opens each morning before the Sun's chariot departs.
Fortune (Fors) is invoked as a power governing outcomes; Phœbus can no longer protect his son by his own power.
Phaëton, son of Phoebus the Sun, begged to drive his father's chariot for a day; he is inexperienced and cannot control the horses.
The Moon is Phœbus's sister, so she is the 'brother' reference here; the Sun's horses normally keep a steady high path.
This catalogue lists mountains across Greece, Asia Minor, Sicily and beyond, many sacred to the Muses, Bacchus or other gods.
The Nile's source was unknown in antiquity, and its delta had seven mouths; Ovid explains both as results of the fire.
Neptune is the god of the sea, brother of Jove; even his power cannot withstand the heat.
This scene follows Phaethon's disastrous drive of the Sun's chariot, which has set the world ablaze; Earth appeals to Jupiter to stop it.
Frankincense was burned as offering to the gods, so Earth notes she supplies even the gods' worship.

literary_notes.text: The poet describes an artwork in detail, using the carvings to display the divine craftsmanship that surpasses its materials.
The sea-nymphs are called neither identical nor different, a gentle observation that makes the carving seem lifelike and natural.
Seasons are shown as attendants with human bodies and traits, each marked by its typical produce or weather.
Phœbus asks what is greater than Jupiter to stress that the task is beyond even the highest god.
Phœbus offers his fear for Phaëton as proof of fatherhood, answering the request for a token with a refusal.
Phaëton's stubbornness against the warnings anticipates his disastrous drive and fall.
Dawn is a goddess opening doors of a palace filled with roses, turning sunrise into a vivid domestic scene.
The father's sighs 'presaging his sorrow' hint that the journey will end in disaster.
Phœbus' warning of 'unfortunately' coveting the chariot anticipates the coming catastrophe, which Phaëton in his youth cannot grasp.
Phaëton rejoices and thanks his reluctant father, joyful just as he leaps toward his doom.
The light chariot is compared to an unballasted ship tossed by waves, making the lack of weight and control vivid.
The narrator turns to address Boötes directly, adding vividness and a touch of humor to the cosmic chaos.
Phaëton's helplessness is compared to a pilot who abandons the helm to the gods in a storm, stressing despair.
The Scorpion is given sweat, menace and a threatening sting, so a star pattern becomes a living monster that terrifies Phaëton.
The ripe grain becomes fuel for its own destruction, turning the harvest into the instrument of its ruin.
The long list of burning mountains conveys the vast scale of the disaster and displays epic learning.
Nymphs with loosened hair mourn their dried springs, giving human grief to the landscape.
The Nile flees and hides his head like a frightened person, explaining the mystery of its source.
'Three times' repeated shows Neptune's failed attempts, stressing the heat's power even over a major god.
Earth is portrayed as a living woman who lifts her face, wrings her hands, trembles and speaks, making the world's suffering vivid and personal.
Earth's accusing questions stress the injustice of rewarding her faithful service with destruction, and strengthen her plea.
Earth shifts from pity to warning, arguing that the fire will also ruin Jupiter's own palace in heaven.
Earth retreating into her own caverns closes the speech with an image of exhaustion and suffocation.
